articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Counter Narcotics and Cyber-related Designations, Amends Russia-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and cyber-related illicit activities. This action underscores the U.S. government's ongoing commitment to disrupting networks that pose threats to national security and financial stability.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued an Illicit Drugs General License to facilitate certain transactions, while also amending a Russia-related General License and publishing new Frequently Asked Questions to provide further guidance to the public regarding the scope and application of these measures.
These measures are part of a broader strategy to combat global illicit finance and cybercrime, aiming to prevent sanctioned actors from exploiting the international financial system.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates New Entities in Counter Terrorism Action
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new designations under its counter terrorism authority. These actions aim to disrupt the financial and logistical support networks of terrorist organizations.
Details of the designated individuals and entities were made public to alert financial institutions and other regulated entities to their obligations under U.S. sanctions law.
These designations reinforce the U.S. government's commitment to combating global terrorism and preventing the flow of funds to those who seek to destabilize international security.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Joint Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a dual action today, designating individuals and entities involved in both counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. This coordinated effort targets illicit networks that often overlap in their operations and funding.
The designations aim to sever financial lifelines and disrupt the logistical capabilities of these dangerous organizations.
This action highlights the U.S. government's comprehensive approach to tackling multifaceted threats to national security and international stability.

articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran Designation List
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an update to its Iran designation list. This action reflects ongoing efforts to address the Iranian regime's destabilizing activities and its support for terrorism.
The update includes modifications to existing entries and may involve new additions or clarifications to previously designated individuals and entities.
Financial institutions and businesses are advised to review the updated list carefully to ensure compliance with U.S. sanctions against Iran.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-related Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new Iran-related designations, targeting individuals and entities associated with the Iranian regime's illicit activities. These actions are part of a continued campaign to exert economic pressure on Iran.
The designations aim to disrupt financial networks that support Iran's proliferation-sensitive nuclear activities, ballistic missile program, and its backing of regional proxy groups.
These measures reinforce the U.S. government's commitment to preventing Iran from acquiring the resources necessary to fund its malign behavior.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Imposes New Cuba Sanctions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced significant designations targeting cyber-related threats and transnational criminal organizations. This action aims to disrupt illicit financial activities and cyber-attacks that pose risks to U.S. national security and economic interests.

In a separate but concurrent action, OFAC also imposed new designations related to Cuba, targeting a crude oil shipping network, state-owned entities, and China-based suppliers of Cuba's military forces.
Additionally, OFAC published a Cuba-related determination, extending Executive Order 14404 to four more sectors of the Cuban economy: manufacturing, technology, electronics, and marine.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-related Designations, Amends Venezuela-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new Iran-related designations and updates to certain Iran-related listings. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to counter the Iranian regime's destabilizing activities.
OFAC also published an Iran-related alert, warning about the Iranian shadow fleet's reliance on false flags for sanctions evasion.
Furthermore, an amended Venezuela-related General License and a new Frequently Asked Question were issued, providing updated guidance on transactions involving Venezuela.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Iran-related General License. This amendment aims to clarify or adjust existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran.
The issuance of amended general licenses is a routine measure to ensure that sanctions programs remain effective while minimizing unintended consequences.
Parties involved in Iran-related transactions are advised to review the updated license carefully to ensure continued compliance.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities Related to North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new designations targeting entities connected to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. These actions aim to counter illicit activities that undermine regional stability and human rights.
The North Korea designations are part of ongoing efforts to disrupt Pyongyang's revenue generation for its weapons programs, including through the exploitation of overseas workers.
The Democratic Republic of the Congo-related designations address concerns about corruption and human rights abuses in the region.

articles.headline: EU Imposes 21st Sanctions Package on Russia, Targeting 113 Individuals and Entities
body: The Council of the European Union has adopted its 21st package of sanctions against Russia, adding 113 individuals and entities to its principal Russia sanctions list. This extensive measure targets those deemed responsible for actions undermining or threatening the territorial integrity, sovereignty, and independence of Ukraine, particularly in response to Russia's attacks on civilian infrastructure.

The new designations include nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions, aiming to further cut off financial channels that fund Russia's war effort. The package also extends restrictions across banking, energy, shipping, and online retail, including the sole shareholder of Russian retail giant Wildberries and an individual controlling a majority stake in Ozon.

Additionally, 32 listings were made under the EU's hybrid and cyber sanctions regimes, targeting individuals and entities involved in foreign information manipulation and interference, and malicious cyber activities. These measures underscore the EU's determination to maintain pressure on Moscow and prevent circumvention of sanctions.

articles.headline: UN Security Council 1718 Sanctions Committee Updates North Korea Sanctions List
body: The UN Security Council 1718 Sanctions Committee has updated one entry on its sanctions list related to the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK). The update pertains to the Mansudae Overseas Project Group of Companies, which has been involved in exporting workers from the DPRK to other nations for construction activities, including statues and monuments, to generate revenue for the DPRK government.
The Mansudae Overseas Project Group of Companies has reportedly conducted business in various countries across Africa and Southeast Asia.
This amendment reflects ongoing international efforts to monitor and enforce sanctions against North Korea to curb its illicit revenue streams that support its nuclear and ballistic missile programs.

articles.headline: BIS Implements New Export Controls on Remote Access to Advanced AI Chips and Rescinds AI Diffusion Rule
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has issued an interim final rule establishing new export licensing requirements for remote access to and exports of advanced-node integrated circuits (AI chips). Effective November 19, 2026, this rule aims to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging U.S. advanced computing power to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.

The new regulations create an end-use control requiring a license to export, reexport, or transfer AI chips to any country if the exporter has 'knowledge' that the item is destined for a data center providing access to more than 12 million 'aggregate TPP' (total processing performance) to or for companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent is headquartered in, Macau or a Country Group D:5 destination, including China.

Additionally, the rule imposes licensing requirements for certain advanced computing items destined for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil, citing a 'higher-than-normal risk of diversion.' The interim final rule also formally rescinds most of the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule, which BIS had previously announced it would not enforce.

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
